items.question: What is a normal inflation rate?
items.answer: Most central banks target 2% annual inflation as an ideal rate  -  high enough to provide a buffer against deflation and support economic growth, but low enough to preserve purchasing power. US inflation averaged approximately 2% to 3% annually for most of the 2010s before rising sharply in 2021 to 2022 and gradually returning toward target levels.

items.question: Why does the government want some inflation?
items.answer: Moderate inflation is considered healthy for several reasons. It gives central banks room to cut interest rates during downturns (harder to do near zero). It encourages spending and investment rather than hoarding cash. It makes debt easier to service over time. Deflation  -  falling prices  -  can be more economically damaging as it creates incentives to delay spending and can trigger a deflationary spiral.

items.question: How does inflation affect interest rates?
items.answer: Central banks raise interest rates to combat high inflation. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, reduce spending and investment, and slow economic activity  -  which reduces upward pressure on prices. When inflation is low or falling, central banks cut rates to stimulate economic activity. The relationship between inflation and interest rates is the primary lever of monetary policy.

items.question: What is hyperinflation?
items.answer: Hyperinflation is an extremely rapid inflation rate  -  conventionally defined as above 50% per month. It typically results from a government printing money to fund spending without adequate economic output to back the currency. Historical examples include Germany in 1923, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, and Venezuela in recent years. Hyperinflation destroys the value of savings and creates economic chaos.

items.question: Is inflation good or bad for homeowners?
items.answer: Generally good in the long term. Home values tend to rise with inflation, increasing the nominal value of the property. The mortgage  -  a fixed nominal debt  -  becomes cheaper to repay in real terms as inflation rises. Homeowners also benefit from locked-in mortgage payments while rents rise with inflation. This is one reason homeownership is often cited as an inflation hedge.
